title: food as practice
hook: pure food, a clear mind, a steady memory, every knot loosened: one chain in the Chandogya

segments.voice: Yesterday, food as practice, and Uddalaka's ember: the mind, my dear, is made of food. Before a meal, did you remember the ember? Day one thousand three hundred thirteen.

Pure food. A clear mind. A steady memory. Every knot loosened. That's a chain, link by link, and it sits at the close of the seventh chapter of the Chandogya Upanishad. The chapter opens with the sage Narada admitting that, for all his learning, he's still in sorrow. It ends with this chain, and with a teacher showing him the far shore beyond darkness. Yesterday a hungry student got his memory back after a meal. Today the same Upanishad takes that thought much further. On the last of our food days, and the end of a week: the chain.
screen: `PURE FOOD, CLEAR MIND.` → `STEADY MEMORY, KNOTS LOOSENED.` → `THE FAR SHORE BEYOND DARKNESS.`

segments.voice: Here's the line, in paraphrase. When food is pure, the inner being is pure. When the inner being is pure, memory becomes steady. When memory is steady, all the knots are loosened. In Sanskrit it begins aharashuddhau sattvashuddhih. Ahara is what's taken in. Sattva is the inner being, the mind in its clearest sense. Notice three things. First, the direction. It runs from the plate inward. Not from a big idea down to the kitchen, but from something as plain as a meal toward something as large as freedom. Second, memory here isn't remembering where the keys are. Readers in the Vedanta tradition take it as a steady remembering of what matters, of who one really is. Third, the knots. The text doesn't name them. Readers have heard in them the tangles that bind a person: craving, confusion, old fears. Every one loosened, the line says. And then the scholar's turn. Shankara, the Vedanta teacher, reads ahara more widely than food. In his reading it's everything gathered in: what the eyes take in, what the ears take in, what the mind is fed all day. Pure intake, not just a pure plate. So the chain reaches into a screen as easily as a kitchen. Now the look back over our food days. Bhrigu's vow: don't speak ill of food. Eating in measure. A meal with the mind on it. The three kinds of food and how you feel an hour later. The guest at the door. The ember. And this chain. And the wider look back, over the lens so far: the doshas, held as a way of noticing; the daily routine; the seasons met with care; and food, from the plate all the way to the knots.
screen: `PURE FOOD, PURE INNER BEING` · `STEADY MEMORY, KNOTS LOOSENED` · `AHARA: ALL THAT'S TAKEN IN` · `FROM THE PLATE TO THE KNOTS`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at today's intake. Sit comfortably and let the breath slow. Go back through the day so far, not only meals. What did the eyes take in? A screen, a street, a face. What did the ears take in? Voices, music, news. Let each one pass by, without grading it. Then notice one knot, somewhere: a tightness that something you took in left behind. Just find it. With each breath out, let it loosen a little, if it will. If you pray, you can hold that knot in prayer. The bell holds the time.
Food as practice. In the Chandogya's chain, pure intake, a clear inner being, steady memory, and every knot loosened. Today's word.
Your line: food as practice. Today, treat one thing you take in through the eyes or ears the way you'd treat a meal: choose it, and take it slowly. Day one thousand three hundred thirteen.

howItsDone: Some Hindus cite the Chandogya's line aharashuddhau sattvashuddhih to explain care about what and how they eat, and Vedanta teachers following Shankara apply it to everything a person takes in through the senses.

fork.setup: you're Narada. you've studied everything there is, and you're still in sorrow. what do you do?
options: go to a teacher and admit it.
fork.reveal: he goes to Sanatkumara and admits he knows only words. the chapter ends with the chain from pure food to loosened knots, and the far shore beyond darkness.

original.note: Sanskrit, Chandogya Upanishad 7.26.2: when what is taken in is pure, the inner being is pure.

trapdoor: what you thought: eat clean, feel better.
what it means: the Chandogya runs a chain from pure food to a clear inner being, a steady memory, and every knot loosened.
what a scholar hears: Shankara reading ahara as all that the senses gather in, so the chain reaches far past the plate.

sources.ref: Chandogya Upanishad 7.1.2–3 (Narada has studied much but knows only words and is in sorrow; he asks Sanatkumara to take him across)

Shankara's commentary on Chandogya Upanishad 7.26.2 (ahara as what is gathered in, the perception of sense objects)

notes: Week end and last food day. The look-back names days 1307–1312 (Bhrigu's vow, measure, eating with attention, the three kinds of food, the guest, the ember) and the Ayurveda lens so far.
Chandogya 7.26.2: confirm the chain 'aharashuddhau sattvashuddhih, sattvashuddhau dhruva smritih, smritilambhe sarvagranthinam vipramokshah' and the paraphrase of sattva as 'the inner being'.
Shankara's reading of ahara as the knowledge or perception of sense objects ('that which is gathered in'): confirm wording.
'Readers have heard in them the tangles that bind a person: craving, confusion, old fears' is an interpretive gloss, attributed to readers, not to the text.
Editor pass: varied the stock 'turn it a few ways' lead-in; attributed the reading of 'steady memory' as remembering who one is to Vedanta readers rather than to the text.
Narada's opening (7.1) paraphrased; 'the far shore beyond darkness' (tamasas param) from 7.26.2.
